What is Refactoring?
Refactoring
is a disciplined technique for restructuring an existing body of code,
altering its internal structure without changing its external behavior.
Each transformation (called a "refactoring") does little, but a sequence of
transformations can produce a significant restructuring.
The goal is to make code
easier to understand
,
cheaper to modify
, and
safer to
extend
.

Why Refactor?
Improves software design
-- Without refactoring, the design of a program will
decay over time.
Makes software easier to understand
-- Code that communicates its purpose

Helps find bugs

Helps you program faster

features.

pages.title: When to Refactor?
lines: : The first time you do something, just do it. The second time, you
wince at duplication but do it anyway. The third time, you refactor.
: Refactor to make the new feature easier to add.
: Refactor to make the bug obvious.
: Refactor to improve readability and maintainability.
pages.text:
When to Refactor?
Rule of Three
: The first time you do something, just do it. The second time, you
wince at duplication but do it anyway. The third time, you refactor.
When adding a feature
: Refactor to make the new feature easier to add.
When fixing a bug
: Refactor to make the bug obvious.
During code review
: Refactor to improve readability and maintainability.

You have an expression that is hard to understand.

pages.title: A4. Inline Temp
lines: You have a temporary variable that is assigned to once with a simple expression, and the
temp is getting in the way of other refactorings.
Replace all references to that temp with the expression.
Inline Temp is most often used as part of Replace Temp with Query, so it may not seem to have value
on its own. But it is useful when the temp is blocking another refactoring.

pages.title: A5. Replace Temp with Query
lines: You are using a temporary variable to hold the result of an expression.
Extract the expression into a method. Replace all references to the temp with the method
call. The new method can then be used in other methods.

pages.title: A7. Remove Assignments to Parameters
lines: A value is assigned to a parameter inside the method's body.
Use a local variable instead of a parameter.
Assigning to parameters is confusing. It blurs the line between input values and local working
variables. It can also prevent certain optimizations and confuse readers about the method's intent.

pages.title: A8. Replace Method with Method Object
lines: A8. Replace Method with Method Object
You have a long method in which local variables are so intertwined that you cannot apply Extract Method.
Transform the method into a separate class so that the local variables become fields of the class. Then you can split
the method into several methods within the same class.
pages.text:
A8. Replace Method with Method Object
Problem:
You have a long method in which local variables are so intertwined that you cannot apply Extract Method.
Solution:
Transform the method into a separate class so that the local variables become fields of the class. Then you can split
the method into several methods within the same class.

pages.title: B1. Move Method
lines: A method is used more by another class than by its own class, or a method uses more
features of another class than the class on which it is defined.
Create a new method in the class that uses the method the most, then either turn the old
method into a delegation or remove it altogether.
pages.text:
B1. Move Method
Problem:
A method is used more by another class than by its own class, or a method uses more
features of another class than the class on which it is defined.
Solution:
Create a new method in the class that uses the method the most, then either turn the old
method into a delegation or remove it altogether.

pages.title: B5. Hide Delegate
lines: A client is calling a delegate class of an object directly.
Create methods on the server to hide the delegate.
Encapsulation is one of the key principles of OOP. When a client needs to call methods on a delegate
object obtained from another object, the client needs to know about the delegate. If the delegate
changes, the client may need to change too.

Create getting and setting methods for the field and use only those to access the field, even
This allows subclasses to override how the field is accessed.

pages.title: C2. Replace Data Value with Object
lines: C2. Replace Data Value with Object
A data item that needs additional data or behavior (e.g., a phone number string that needs
formatting, validation, or area code extraction).
Turn the data item into an object.
In early stages of development, simple data items represented as Strings or numbers are fine. As the
system grows, these simple items often need formatting, validation, or associated behavior. At that
point, wrap them in an object.

complexity of managing its lifecycle.
Solution:
Make it a value object.

lines: C7. Change Unidirectional Association to Bidirectional
You have two classes that need to use each other's features, but only a one-way link exists.
Add back pointers, and change modifiers to update both sets.
When class A references class B, but class B also needs to know about class A, add a back-pointer
from B to A and manage the link from both sides.

F10. Form Template Method
Problem:
You have two methods in subclasses that perform similar steps in the same order, yet the
steps are different.
Solution:
Get the steps into methods with the same signature, so that the original methods become
the same. Then pull them up into the superclass using the Template Method pattern.
The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a superclass and lets subclasses
override specific steps. If subclasses have similar overall structure but differ in details, Form Template
Method can unify the structure.

Refactoring Best Practices
1.
Always have tests
before refactoring -- refactoring without tests is risky
2.
Small steps
-- each refactoring should be a small, verifiable change
3.
Commit frequently
-- after each successful refactoring step
4.
Do not add functionality
while refactoring -- separate concerns
5.
Follow your nose
-- if code smells, investigate and refactor
6.
Use IDE support
-- automated refactoring tools reduce manual errors
7.
Review the result
-- ensure the refactored code is actually better
